When ten-year-old Rick Baker first began experimenting with the most basic of makeup materials, his emerging passion for the sorts of illusions which could be wrought with these arcane substances was decidedly out of the ordinary. Motion picture makeup-the kind that transforms actors into monsters, aliens or even animals - was not at all the stellar occupation it has come to be; and at the time, there was little in the way of instructional materials an enthusiastic novice could draw upon, let alone a clearly marked path toward professional involvement. Baker's unwavering dedication, coupled with a single-minded pursuit of excellence, was to serve him well, however - vaulting him past such obstacles to a position of prominence in a burgeoning career field in which he now has few peers. From the early, low-budget efforts of Octoman and Schlock, through It's Alive and The Incredible Melting Man, and eventually on to loftier assignments in Star Wars, The Incredible Shrinking Woman and the lamentable King Kong remake, Baker honed his skills and developed his talents - ultimately reaching full maturity in response to the diverse challenges of An American Werewolf in London, Videodrome and Greystoke. From simple pie dough makeups to the most complicated of bodily transformations, Baker delves into his life and work, offering an incisive look at the artist and his art. Article by Jordan Fox. MAKER OF MONSTERS RICK BAKER MASTER OF THE APES

Monday, March 29, 1982. The fifty-fourth annual Academy Awards ceremony has the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion packed, once again, with the customary crowd of tuxedoed and haute coutured actors, producers, directors, and other film industry luminaries. But there is at least one difference this year-the rare addition of a new, regular awards category, one long fought for and hard won. Makeup. It is long overdue. The history of movies is as thoroughly intertwined with the art of makeup as it is with photography, or any of film's other constituent arts. Whether the realistic alteration of actors into screen characters whose physical appearance is taken for granted by audiences, or the memorable fantasy creations that never were and never could be-except on celluloid - the credit belongs to a special breed of artist wielding talent and available technology in equal measure. While there have been two or three special Oscars for makeup in the history of the awards, this is the first annual award -the first time the makeup category has been officially recognized as deserving coequal status. The award is prefaced by a brief presentation on the history of film makeup. Then the first-ever winner is announced. For An American Werewolf in LondonRick Baker. Baker steps forward, thanks his parents, comments on what the award means to him and salutes grandmaster of the field Dick Smith. It is an emotional moment, both at the podium and for several members of the audience-among them friends and colleagues, some of whom have occasion to think back sixteen years to recall a fourteen-year-old kid from Covina, California, with a knack for making rubber masks and a fierce desire to be one of the best makeup artists the field has ever known. Born in upstate New York in 1950, Rick Baker began to follow, at a very young age, the course that would make his life and chosen career two sides of the same coin. His specific, steadfast pursuit of a makeup career may not have begun until the advanced age of fourteen, but the development of necessary skills began much earlier, and the roots of an enduring passion go back earlier still. "I wasn't the average little kid in my neighborhood," Baker noted. "I really liked monsters and monster movies-even the cheap, crummy ones." Monster-from the Latin monstrum, meaning something of such hideous appearance and unfriendly intent as to prompt feelings of shock, fear and revulsion. And from the 1896 Edison production of Frankenstein on, both a mainstay of cinema and a major raison d'etre of the makeup man's art. The young Rick Baker could seldom slake this fascination at the local movie house, but television brought a steady parade of imaginationsparking monsters into his living room. "I was fortunate to have such understanding parents. They could easily have started to wonder. I mean, it's pretty weird for a kid to be that interested in this stuff. We were a very normal lower middle class family, but my parents were never the type to say, 'No, you can't watch those awful horror movies!' " For a while, the young enthusiast had little notion as to who might be responsible for these grotesque creations, supposing perhaps that Boris Karloff had somehow managed to make himself look that way. Wanting to know more about this, he asked his father, who told him that an artist was responsible. "My dad is a very creative person who never had the chance to develop his creativity when he was young because he had to quit school early and help support his family. He understood that my interest was a serious one, and that it might lead somewhere." His father's belief had some basis in fact, as Baker had already shown considerable drawing ability. But I don't know if it's something you have to be born with. Part of what being an artist is is just being able to really see things. My father helped me to see things, and to analyze why they looked the way they did: 'The light's coming from over there, so it's casting a shadow over here. " With some greasepaint his father got for him, Baker was able to do some crude makeups on himself, of the vampire and zombie variety. Very quickly, he was looking ahead to the next stage, whatever that might be. From devouring copies of Famous Monsters magazine-curiously enough, a major early inspiration for several of today's prominent filmmakers- Baker knew that something else was missing, something three-dimensional. There was little money available for acquiring makeup supplies to experiment with, but he continued to receive his parent's encouragement. Some basic makeup books from the library helped, and soon Baker had taught himself the rudiments of nose-putty makeups. (Pie dough, he found, tinted with food coloring, was an inexpensive substitute.) The primary object, at least at first, was to have the makeup stick to his face long enough to take a snapshot of it. Little Rick Baker was a real shy kid, very quiet-the kind of 'How come this kid's so nice kid who'd make other parents say, and quiet, when ours can't sit still?' I spent a lot of time in my room, doing these crude makeups. Another attraction of the makeup was that with a monster face, this shy kid could do things that Rick Baker couldn't do without it. Most of the kids from the old neighborhood are probably in jail today, so all that time spent in my room may have been fortunate in other ways." Another book revealed the secrets of slush-casting a nose piece, and making simple slip-rubber masks. Both techniques use a sulfur-containing rubber that cures by itself upon prolonged exposure to air and the absorbent plaster of a mold. A filler material in the mix gives the rubber more shape-retaining properties. In slip-casting -a term borrowed from pottery-making, with the rubber being comparable to a clay slurry - a mold would normally be filled with the liquid latex, with moisture gradually drawn off by the plaster, leaving an even build-up of rubber 'skin' on the inner surface of the mold. The excess liquid left inside is then dumped out, and the mask removed. Its thickness is determined by the length of time the mixture has been left in the mold. When done properly, the result is a hollow latex mask, like the readymade masks which can be purchased in many novelty shops. But this procedure, like the successive pour-and-slush method, was much too wasteful of the precious slip-rubber. Baker quickly learned that sculpting would be the most vital skill for a creator of makeups to master. In the final analysis, results could be no better than the three-dimensional designs from which they sprang. Also of great importance was the ability to translate a design into a usable mold in which to make the rubber piece or mask. Baker did most of his early sculpting, in clay, over the plastic head and face that came in an anatomical model kit called 'The Visible Head.' "The earliest molds I made from these were basically one-piece, and they were terrible. The very first one I remember was actually made by my dad-again figuring things out without any instructions to go by. We went to a local hardware store and bought a little box of patching plaster-the kind you'd use for a wall. It sets up very quickly, so it was always a race to get the plaster on the sculpture before it set up. You'd be throwing big gobs of this stuff on with both hands, and there'd be air pockets all over the place." Baker's first mask was produced in this manner at the age of twelve or thirteen, though he had turned out smaller slip-rubber pieces even earlier. Although he was quite dissatisfied with the outcome of his early efforts - an attempted wolfman, colored with food coloring, for instance-it was nonetheless an exciting time. An early stab at a larger mask was a rough approximation of the makeup worn by Christopher Lee in Hammer's Curse of Frankenstein. "The only texture it had," Baker laughs, "was my As with every skill or technique he would work at developingfrom the earliest times on- Baker kept at it tenaciously until his progress offered sufficient encouragement to warrant moving on to the next phase. But while his slip-rubber masks would gradually improve on the outside, he realized that even better ones would require that they be made to fit the wearer's face. To do that, one needed a lifemask. The latter-a thin plaster impression of the individual contours of the subject's face - pointed the way to better molds. Gradual developments of these moldmaking procedures-some derived from books, but much of it reasoned out on his own - became a major focus of Baker's self-taught makeup education, up until his exposure to the advanced, professional techniques of Dick Smith. When Baker first began using a lifemask to make better, formfitting latex masks, he ran into serious problems. "My first masks based on a lifemask were done with a plaster of paris lifemask of me taken by my father. It wasn't even full-face. A bit later on, after we'd learned some more from makeup books, he took another impression that went much farther back." In the lifemask-which could be called the 'first negative mold'-Baker cast up a plaster positive duplicate of his face. Over that, he would sculpt the 'mask face' in clay, then put the whole assemblage down on the counter and cover it with more plaster to make a negative mold of his sculpture. "When it came time to take it apart, I had this face-cast encased in plaster, with no handle or any way to pull it out. It would take hours to try and pry the damn thing apart without breaking the sides of the mold off." THE AUVENTURES OF Caprain ALTION

Sometimes the mold-as well as the sculpture underneathcould not be saved, and he was lucky just to save the lifemask. for some reason, this hadn't been a problem when he'd used the smooth, bland, nearly-featureless 'Visible Head' as a basis, rather than the plaster replica of his own face. Rick Baker had discovered 'undercuts.' As a more apparent example of an undercut, imagine an attempt to cast up a solid sphere. Unless the mold happened to be divided into perfect hemispheres, it would be impossible to remove without causing damage. The 'short' side would come off readily, but the larger section would be wrapped around the sphere's 'equator'-an undercut. This same principle applies to parts of a face-cast: under the nose; with prominent cheekbones; around and under the jaw, especially; and even with surface textures, such as a sculpted wrinkle. Subsequent exposure to more advanced moldmaking procedures would resolve this problem. Even the most prodigious talent can scarcely emerge in a vacuum. On film, there were the results of makeup handiwork - some of it good, most of it not. There were also things he could learn with his father's assistance, or by trial and error, or from what few books he could find. But better sources of information and inspiration were needed. Such a source appeared early-on in the person of Bob Burns. Though Burns is perhaps best known today as a leading collector of fantasy-film props and artifacts, his involvement with makeup extends back to childhood. Stymied in his own efforts to pursue a makeup career when he sought admission to the union in 1955, Burns became a protege of the late Paul Blaisdell-an independent creator of crude monster suits for early Roger Corman films, who nevertheless always managed adequate results on nonexistent budgets- assisting Blaisdell on Invasion of the Saucer Men and other vintage programmers. Drafted into the Army in 1958, Burns had a chance to use his makeup skills on Army training films, creating gruesome casualty wounds that had to appear as realistic as possible. Whenever doctors or medics new to the service threw up while viewing these films, Burns reckoned his work must have been successful. From the time Bob Burns left the Army, up until the late 1960s, makeup artists were scarcely in any sort of spotlight, and the work of Hollywood professionals-with rare exceptionsremained shrouded in secrecy. Certainly, there were no such working professionals a thirteen-year-old maker of slip-rubber masks could approach. But Famous Monsters had run two articles on Burns, which made him out to be a very friendly and accessible person. Though Burns had forsaken the pursuit of a makeup career to become a film editor, he was then still helping out part-time at Don Post Studios painting masks and doing hair-work, just to keep his hand in. It was there that Ralph Baker took his son, equipped with sketches and other samples of his work, to meet Burns. "You could see the promise right away," Burns recalled. The two hit it off immediately, and over the next few years Burns became a significant factor in Rick Baker's life. He would bring things in and want me to critique the work. I gave him honest answers, because those are the only kind that help you. Rick was an easy-going kid, and easy to like, yet at the same time he had a real drive to accomplish things. He was pushing himself all the time." Burns claims no credit for what would become one major thread winding through Baker's career, but the 'Kogar' gorilla suit Burs had - which he'd worn in the obscure Ray Dennis Steckler film, Rat Phink and Boo Boo-surely spurred an existing fascination. The way apes had been depicted in countless horror and adventure films had easily qualified them as honorary monsters in the eyes of a pre-teen Rick Baker. A few years later, seriously trying his hand at a variety of more difficult makeup challenges, he'd find that a gorilla neatly fit in with some of the things which had most attracted him to makeup in the first place-a desire to fool people, which called for the creation of things that could Baker found the Kogar suit entertaining in appearance, but was far from satisfied with its convincingness. Through Burns, he learned about the notable ape-impersonators in film history - Ray 'Crash' Corrigan, George Barrows and especially Charles Gemora. A seed was planted. One day Rick Baker would build a gorilla suit that would satisfy the most critical observerThe long path to greater realism, Baker realized, lay in returning to the source. And so-besides his regular method of carefully noting all the deficiencies of every manufactured example he saw - Rick began a long-term researching of the real animal. He scoured library shelves for books on the subject, kept a lookout for National Geographic issues that might have something of interest, and began to haunt the local zoo. Contrary to the monster or 'heavy' image fostered by Hollywood, he discovered a magnificent, gentle and reclusive creature. To start with, however, Baker just wanted to build something along the lines of Kogar. "The biggest problem for a thirteenyear-old kid wanting to build his own gorilla suit was money," he recalled. Cost and knowledge factors forced him to stick with a head for the time being. His first attempt was simply a gorillahead, built up out of sheet foam, self-curing latex and cotton. It had a partially moveable jaw. He went through three or four more like that, before deciding to sculpt one and cast it. The first sculpted head was dubbed 'Jombo.' Over a period of time, Baker added glove-hands, basic arms and chest-using some simple padding his mother had helped him make-covered with a cheap fake fur material. The lack of a lower half to the suit was glossed over by the simple expedient of having the gorilla wear a large pair of overalls, much as George Barrows had done for an episode of The Beverly Hillbillies. Given the serious limitations on what he could then manage to build, the suit satisfied him for a time, and he put the ape efforts aside for a few years, in favor of other makeup interests. When Baker reached the age of fifteen, and had the beginnings of a portfolio he and Burns thought could be shown around, Burs used a personal connection to get his young protege an appointment with the Hollywood makeup union's business agent. By doing so, they hoped to get at least some idea what the prospects were and what steps the young enthusiast should take in order to seriously pursue a career in the field. In essence, the union representative told the obviously talented teenager to forget it. Studio makeup departments were no more, so apprenticeships were no more, so there was no way for him to gain admittance to the union and get his professional start. Furthermore, in the agent's estimation, Baker clearly did not have 'what it takes' to be a makeup artist. Although Baker later came to realize that what he'd been told was in fact motivated by the fear of competition from talented new blood, it is a mark of the conviction and resolve he possessed even then that he shrugged off this 'advice,' when most others might have been crushed by it. For his part, Burns got a distinct feeling of deja vu from this incident, but he'd received the brush-off as an adult. If anything, however, the experience only served to reinforce Baker's determination that, no matter the obstacles, nothing would keep him from achieving his goal, except the limits of his ability. A key creative influence who came to overshadow what someone like Bob Burns could offer Rick Baker, soon arrived-first in the example, then the person, of Dick Smith. Smith, the dean of modern makeup artists, responsible for numerous state-ofthe-art innovations and many of the best character and special effects makeups of the last twenty years, was the subject of a few Famous Monsters articles, and had even authored a couple himself, presenting 'how to' information on some of his creations. This openness with information, the impact of great designs brought to life, and Smith's penchant for realism-basing, for example, his Quasimodo makeup on two actual diseases that could lead to such deformities- made an instant and ardent fan of young Rick Baker. For some time, he waivered over whether or not to write Smith. "I thought: 'Here's this famous professional. Why should he care about some kid in Covina? Someday, if I do something I think is pretty good, maybe I'll send him some pictures -pictures that would speak better than anything I could The 1965 publication of Monster Makeup Handbook, written by Smith during an unexpected lull in his film career, added more fuel to the fire. In fact, its impact could hardly have been bested had someone detonated a bomb in Baker's backyard. Instead of the relatively sketchy information contained in magazine articles, here were detailed step-by-step procedures for creating a wide range of makeups, utilizing techniques and materials that

were within the reach of dedicated hobbyists. Baker well recalls his first reaction on learning of Smith's book. He was working on some makeups for his freshman high school drama class when a classmate asked if he had gleaned a certain trick from the Dick Smith handbook, which he had seen in a local store. "All at once, I said: 'What?! Are you sure about this? Where'd you see it? How many copies were left?' I got so excited, I wanted to run right out and get one, but that was the first class of the day. I couldn't concentrate on school at all that day. What if they were sold out?! After the last class, I ran to the store and bought a couple copies. It was an incredible find! Dick's explanations were so much clearer than what I'd seen, and he gave you what you needed to do a lot of specific makeups." Baker all but devoured the Dick Smith handbook. Its projects ranged from the fairly easy to the moderately difficult. But, according to Burns, it was uncanny how closely Baker's results duplicated the photos of even the more difficult makeups. The articles and the handbook comprised Rick Baker's first exposure to more professional approaches to sculpting, use of lifemasks and moldmaking. And he continued to learn and to experiment on his own over the next year and a half, filling in the gaps where he could with independently-reasoned makeshift solutions. School came to seem less and less relevant. A secondary interest Baker had had from an early age-spurred by movies like The 7th Voyage of Sinbad-was model animation. Seeing some relation between the three-dimensional models one had to move in order to create an illusion of life and his early efforts at sculpting, he'd borrowed an old hand-wound Brownie camera from his father and started to experiment. The camera was on its last legs, and his most careful attempts to shoot one frame often resulted in ten or twelve clicking through the gate. While animation was fun to do, Baker did not find his amateur footage encouraging, "I didn't have the patience for it, or the frame memory. Makeup had much more immediate results." Still, the world of animation and animators cropped up again, significantly, in the formative stages of Baker's career. While still in high school, he decided to look for part-time employment. None of the jobs traditionally open to teenagers seemed appealing and, lacking a car, he was limited to something in the immediate area. One of his father's jobs occasionally took the senior Baker next door to Clokey Productions, where Gumby and the Davey and Goliath TV series were made. Going there one day with some of his masks and small sculptures, Rick Baker was hired on the spot. He first went to work in the art department as a general purpose artist, sculptor, prop- and moldmaker. Most of the prominent young model animators had worked at the Clokey shop at one time or another. Jim Danforth and David Allen were gone by the time Baker arrived; but through others still working at the facility, this group of animators became Baker's first friends and associates in the film business. He credits them, in fact, with teaching him many useful and unfamiliar techniques for sculpting, molding and casting. Fellow Clokeyite Doug Beswick, who became a close friend, introduced him to foam rubber and its oven-curing procedures. Baker had known of this mysterious generic substance, so indispensible to the making of modern prosthetic appliances, but had previously shied away from it due to a lack of the special equipment required and apprehension over the difficulties of working with it. Usage of the foamed rubber for animation models and makeup purposes were parallel, but not the same. For animation models, the volume of air beaten into the rubber mixture was less, because of the puppet's much denser hide; the animators' molds were much cruder and sloppier, with imperfect castings of lesser importance, because most of the detail work-often extending to major changes- was done later; and there was no need for blending edges, as with prosthetic pieces. Relieved that working with foam was not as complicated as he'd supposed, Baker began to use the rubber also for makeup purposes. At first, he concentrated on full-face masks, along the lines of those he'd made earlier using the far simpler slip techniques. Somes of these, he still feels-such as some Neanderthal caveman masks, made for a 16mm stop-motion short he and Beswick started but never finished-were "not bad, for the time." Foam appliances, however, were something he was just beginning to make at age eighteen, around the end of the year he worked at Clokey's. Not knowing the proper methods for making this type of mold, Baker improvised his own. These halting first steps into appliance manufacture were taken at home, rather than with the professional equipment at the animation shop. "It made the whole house smell like burning rubber. You don't want to put a turkey in the kitchen oven after you've just baked some foam. Like I said, I wouldn't be here today if I hadn't had very understanding parents." Finally armed with what he considered more presentable samples of his work- including some derived from Dick Smith makeups-Baker sent a letter and stack of photos off to the makeup artist. Much to his surprise, a return envelope came back, and quickly. Inside it were a reject foam casting of the Quasimodo-like makeup from television's Way Out series, early test photos of the Little Big Man age makeup, and a most encouraging letter, containing an invitation to visit Smith, if and when his young admirer made it back East. Coincidentally, Baker was to receive a trip to New York as a high school graduation present, and so it was with great anticipation that he made plans to add one extra stop to the round of visits with relatives. When Baker did meet the artist, he assumed he'd be in store for little more than a brief tour of Smith's studio. But he was hardly through the door when Smith handed him a notepad. When Baker inquired what it was for, he was told, "I'm going to tell you a lot of things, and I want you to remember them." Surprised again, but clearly delighted, Baker remained from morning until night, jotting notes on all sorts of formulas and processes. "He told me everything he possibly could. I overcame my shyness enough to ask questions, 'How do you make a wrinkle look that good in the sculpting?,' and so on. Dick was so free with the information. He'd been kind of shy too as a kid, and didn't get into makeup until a later age. Baker had found a mentor in the maverick East Coast makeup artist-though Smith insists the emphasis in that description be placed on 'friend and advisor,' rather than 'instructor.' But the admiration did not all run one-way. "Rick impressed me enormously, said Smith. "Occasionally, I had met young people who were interested in makeup, and had even tried to find some as far back as my early days in the makeup department at NBC. But I had never encountered any who had a real gift for makeup. Rick was the first one. He obviously had great artistic talent, and it was also clear that he loved makeup and was single-minded about it. He had, at that age, reached a level of proficiency that I don't suppose I had reached until I'd been working professionally for several years. Even as a teenager, he was certainly more capable than the average makeup artist." The information Baker harvested from this initial visit was enough to keep him busy for a long time to come. He could not wait to get back to California to get started. An active correspondence with Smith continued over the next few years, but the young devotee made a point of not taking a vexing technical problem to Smith until he had exhausted his own attempts at finding a solution. Smith even made arrangements for Baker to sit in as an observer on Little Big Man and several other assignments he undertook on the West Coast. The basic moldmaking procedures Baker came to employ were refined over many years by Dick Smith, from methods used earlier by George Bau and Gustaf Norin. But prior to his acquaintance with Smith, Baker had improvised his own methods, which were curiously similar to the no-longer-state-of-the-art techniques then prevalent in Hollywood. "When Dick first saw one of my molds, he was impressed that I'd figured out this way of doing it on my own. Baker's early lifemasks were first sunk into a plaster baseplate formed within a shallow box made of wood. The sculpture was then rendered over the plaster-mounted lifemask, and the negative mold made from this, but made to cover the entire baseplate, to which it was securely joined by 'keys.' Compared with Smith's technique, such molds were relatively simple to make, but were big and blocky, instead of a typically faceshaped oval. Also, their greater amount of plaster held a substantially greater risk of misfit, warpage and other problems. It was an approach geared towards making a whole mask, and it served that purpose effectively. Baker found, however, that more realistic makeups were based on overlapping appliances-and Smith's methods were particularly well-suited to making superior appliances. After the sculpture stage, the face is generally divided into several constituent parts for individual casting. (Smith used as many as fifteen for the Little Big Man age makeup.) This in turn allows exact and varying thicknesses for different pieces, far better blending edges for the appliances and more precise application of the makeup. Explains Baker,iYou can get in there and glue down every fraction of an inch of that surface, and do it well." A defective piece is also more easily replaced. An extra bonus is that such molds have lasting value. Certain appliances like eye bags and neck pieces may be a good fit on another actor years later, when time is too short for custom work. Many makeup artists try to keep a 'library' of these molds, accumulated over the course If what is to be made involves any more than the subject's face, a bald cap-made from a resinous substance - is affixed to provide a flush working surface and to keep materials out of the hair. Alginate, a semi-hard, gelatinous material derived from seaweed, is applied over the face to form a negative mold for the lifemask. Used also by dentists for taking impressions of teeth, alginate has become the standard material for lifemask preparation- replacing plaster of paris, which was abrasive and heavy, stuck to the skin, and gave off heat as it hardened. To reinforce the outside, four layers of wet plaster-bandage-each bandage about a sixteenth of an inch thick-are applied over the quarter-inch thickness of alginate. To insure tight contact, the bandages are 'worked into' the alginate, leaving no valleys or air pockets. Any problems due to uneven distribution of the alignate are corrected in the same manner. The lifemask is also extended further back, towards the ears, so that its cast duplicate will not be too shallow. To cast up the 'new and improved' positive, a flexible moldmaking material is used - a silicone or RTV (room-temperature vulcanizing) synthetic rubber which, after the addition of a catalyst, will self-cure in the air. And Baker, who would visit Bau at his Laurel Canyon home, found him a wealth of great stories about makeup in 'the old days.' Foam rubber-once known as sponge rubber because of the air micro-encapsulated within its porous cell-structure- was initially the result of experimentation by rubber companies., In use by makeup artists since at least The Wizard of Oz, it has been -until very recently -the only material that could mimic the appearance and tensile properties of real flesh. There have been a number of different formulations over the years, each having certain ingredients in common- a latex base of some sort; a sulfur dispersion to 'cure' the rubber; a zinc dispersion; a gelling agent -but the relative proportions varied greatly, as did the results. "In the beginning," Baker recounted, "working with the foam was haphazard. The makeup men of that time didn't weigh the ingredients out. They just guessed, pouring in a bit of this and little of that, whipping it up and cooking it. Some days it worked great; some days it didn't work at all." What in time became the dominant foam used in Hollywood was a commercial preparation made by Uniroyal. It contained a base of partly synthesized rubber and had certain properties not helpful for makeup purposes. Bau developed his own formula based on all-natural gum latex, with some superplasticizing agent which has never been identified. Custom-made for makeup purposes, Bau's formula yielded a foam rubber unmatched in its simulation of the suppleness and elasticity of real skin. Passing through the makeup departments of various studios from 1939 on, George Bau found the superior appliances he could make with this formulation widely admired-one of the reasons he established his makeup supply sideline. But Bau foam never achieved more than minority use-something Baker attributes to professional jealousy. For many years prior to about 1975, its main proponent was the East Coast-based Dick Smith. Two unrelated, but cumulative, disasters struck in 1974. First, Uniroyal ceased making its foam preparation when polyurethane displaced foam rubber as the standard mattress and cushion material. Its industrial use was now obsolete, and no other company would bother to keep it available just for a handful of makeup artists. Then, deeply depressed at the realization that his comeback in the makeup field was never going to happen, George Bau committed suicide. Shocked upon receiving the news, Baker remembers thinking: "It's all over now. We're going to have to go back to nose putty." For a while, he remained unaware that he had-by the sheerest coincidence-been a catalyst to the field's salvation. Schram was impressed by the facial appliance of the original 'Blockhead,' and wanted to know the source of the rubber used. He was resistent, however, when Baker identified it as the Bau formula, repeating the long-circulating stories that Bau's was just the old Uniroyal foam with mineral oil mixed in to partly break down the rubber for additional plasticity, and that it was unusually foul-smelling and overpriced to boot. Finally, after Baker kept insisting that it was a completely different formula and that he should at least try it, Schram purchased the chemicals-but not the special base-for a test. When a foam-rubber piece comes out of its mold, the latex itself usually has a whitish to yellowish coloration. While appliance finishing generally has to be doné on the actor, normal film makeup has a mineral oil base which attacks rubber. Bau therefore devised a special rubber mask greasepaint based on castor oil. A base coat of the dominant skin tone is first patted in with a stipple sponge. Color highlights are added next with a special brush. Tiny dots of color, picked up by the open-celled stipple sponge, comprise the fine detail. A further complication is the difference between what the human eye sees and what film emulsions record. Rubber reflects light differently than flesh, and while a viewer's eye will compensate for this, the camera tends to 'read' the rubber as being more grey. As the makeup is quite greasy on the rubber, it must be 'set' to achieve a flesh-like sheen without actually being shiny. One technical footnote to Baker's year-long labors on Greystoke may have far-reachings implications for the future of makeup. Though the foam-rubber 'front' had finally been secured, another threat still remained-the unpredictability and short-lived nature of even the best moldmaking plaster. That, compounded by the great size of many of the Greystoke molds sent Baker and his chief moldmaker, Kenny Clarke, on a search for workable alternatives. Ensuing experiments turned up a type of silicone mold, along with a heat- and warp-resistant fiberglass. "We used to think," said Baker, "that the only mold material you could put in the oven-the only kind foam rubber would work in-was plaster. But now we know otherwise. Back at Clokey's, I'd seen silicone molds run of the dog Goliath. It had worked, but there were problems. Still, both materials were used extensively and successfully on Greystoke.
